drafts.neutral_framing: Should Smith County publish its payments — who was paid, how much, and for what — as data anyone can download and search?
drafts.final_wording: Smith County posts its budget, but no check register was found online. Should the county publish every payment as open data anyone can download and search?
drafts.final_wording_note: Framed around a step the county can take on its own: publishing records it already keeps, in a format that meets the Texas Comptroller’s own transparency standard.
shaping_notes: A question about the county’s own disclosure format — not about any person, candidate, or ballot measure. Clears the bright lines.

Grounded in what was and was not found: the county posts budget books and its audit report is online (on a commissioner’s site), but no check register or open spending portal was found (Docket #7). Tarrant County posts a downloadable check register.
drafts.tier_note: Open as a Tier 0 sentiment poll: no account, one voice per browser, changeable until close. Tier 0 is displayed but never cited as verified resident opinion — verification tiers arrive with the full voting layer.
drafts.background: Smith County’s FY27 budget is $198 million, and its property-tax collections have grown every year since FY24. The budget books show how much each office is given. They do not show what was bought. No county check register or open spending portal was found in our search (Docket #7) — that means not found yet, not hidden. Some Texas counties post every payment as downloadable data, and the Texas Comptroller gives a Transparency Star for it.

founding_solutions.title: Publish the check register as open data, like Tarrant County
founding_solutions.summary: Post each month’s payments — vendor, amount, date, and what was bought — as a downloadable spreadsheet, covering at least the last three fiscal years. That meets the Texas Comptroller’s Contracts & Procurement Transparency Star criteria.
